summary: Describes how RTP is used in the context of CLUE, and the recommended ways to map RTP media streams described in SDP to CLUE media captures and scenes. This helps receivers know which incoming stream corresponds to which camera view. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: A room with many cameras sends many video streams. This document explains how to put a name tag on each stream so the other side knows which camera it came from.

questions: how are rtp streams mapped to clue captures
subtitle: How a receiver of a switched telepresence video stream learns which camera is on screen right now.

tldr.problem: When a Multiple Content Capture switches between several original cameras, the receiver cannot tell from the RTP stream alone which original Media Capture it is seeing, so it cannot apply that capture's spatial information such as scaling.
tldr.mechanism: Each Capture Encoding is sent as its own RTP stream, and the sender labels the current original capture with a CaptureID carried in a new RTCP SDES item and in an RTP header extension.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can look up the right capture attributes at any moment. The mapping works only for a single switched-in capture, not for composed streams, which use a single dash as the CaptureID.

today: RFC 8849 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the framework in RFC 8845.

sections.title: RTP and CLUE Media Captures
sections.content:
The CLUE Framework (RFC 8845) defines a Media Capture as a source of media, and a Multiple Content Capture (MCC) as a special capture composed of multiple other captures. Media itself travels in RTP (RFC 3550), where each RTP stream has a unique Synchronization Source (SSRC) in its RTP session, and SDP describes the streams.

Systems that support CLUE use RTP for the media, SDP for codec and transport negotiation, and the CLUE protocol for describing and selecting captures. To tie these together, three mappings are needed: CLUE individual encodings to SDP, RTP streams to SDP (not CLUE-specific), and RTP streams to the current Media Capture inside an MCC. This document covers how RTP and RTCP should be used and how the last mapping is signaled.
sections.eli5: CLUE describes the cameras, and RTP carries the pictures. This document is the glue that tells you which picture belongs to which camera.

sections.title: RTP Topologies for CLUE
sections.content:
The relevant RTP topologies from RFC 7667 are Point-to-Point, Media-Mixing Mixers, Media-Switching Mixers and Selective Forwarding Middleboxes. In Point-to-Point, one peer talks directly to another over unicast, with one or more RTP sessions, each on a separate 5-tuple with its own SSRC space. Peers learn the SSRCs from RTCP Source Description (SDES) reports carrying the Canonical Name (CNAME).

Even a call that is point-to-point at a high level can contain a stream best described by a mixer topology, for example an endpoint that produces composite or switched captures for a receiver with fewer displays than the sender has cameras. In the media mixer topology, peers talk only to the mixer, which sends mixed or composited streams using its own SSRC.
sections.eli5: Sometimes two rooms talk straight to each other, and sometimes a middle box mixes everyone together. Each setup labels its video streams a little differently.

sections.title: Mapping Capture Encodings to RTP Streams
sections.content:
Each Capture Encoding MUST be sent as a separate RTP stream. CLUE endpoints MUST support sending each such stream in its own RTP session signaled by an SDP m= line, and MAY support sending some or all streams in one RTP session using the mechanism in RFC 8843. When each encoding has its own session, the receiver identifies it by port, and the SDP label attribute names the Media Capture in the CLUE description (see RFC 8848).

MCCs add a problem. A consumer that asked for an MCC receives a stream, but the original captures inside it have no Capture Encoding of their own, so they cannot be matched to an m= line by a label. The consumer still needs to know which original capture it is seeing, for instance to get correct scaling information, which can differ between the contributing captures.
sections.eli5: Normally each camera gets its own pipe, and a label on the pipe says which camera it is. A switching feed is trickier, because the camera behind the pipe keeps changing.

sections.title: The Constituent CaptureID
sections.content:
To fix this, the RFC defines an RTP header extension and an RTCP SDES item carrying the captureID of the original capture currently switched into the MCC. This temporarily links the SSRC of the stream to that one capture, so the consumer can use its original attributes, such as spatial information.

The rules depend on how many captures are in the MCC at once. If there is only one, the media provider MUST send its captureID in both the header extension and the SDES item, and MUST send the new value whenever it switches. If more than one is composed into the MCC, the provider MUST NOT send captureIDs this way, although it MAY send them in RTCP SDES packets for the CSRC values when the stream carries Contributing Source information.

If a provider switches from one capture to a composed stream in the same MCC, it MUST send the special value a single dash character. The consumer then treats any earlier CaptureID for that SSRC as no longer applying. A dash cannot be a real captureID because RFC 8846 defines the syntax as xs:ID.
sections.eli5: A camera operator holds up a card with the current camera's name. If several cameras are blended together, they hold up a card with just a dash, meaning no single name applies.

sections.title: SDES Item and Header Extension
sections.content:
The new RTCP SDES item has item type 14, a length, and a CaptureID that is a variable-length UTF-8 string, either a CaptureID negotiated in the CLUE protocol or the single dash character. It MUST be sent in an SDES packet within a compound RTCP packet, unless Reduced-Size RTCP (RFC 5506) has been negotiated, in which case it can be in a noncompound packet.

The same value is also carried in an RTP header extension (RFC 8285), using the mechanism of RFC 7941. Support is negotiated in SDP with the URN urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:CaptureID. The header extension exists because, for switched captures, receivers need to know the original capture to apply geometric adjustments correctly. It need not be on every packet: senders MAY send it only when a new capture is switched in, and then SHOULD send it in the first few RTP packets to reduce the risk of losing it.

IANA registered the extension URI urn:ietf:params:rtp-hdrext:sdes:CaptId and the SDES item type value 14 with abbreviation CCID and name CLUE CaptId.
sections.eli5: The name card can be written in two places: in a regular status report and on the video packets themselves. Sending it on the first few packets after a switch makes sure it is not lost.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
CLUE endpoints MUST support RTP/SAVPF and SRTP (RFC 3711), and DTLS and DTLS-SRTP for keying. All media channels SHOULD be secure unless the RTP and RTCP are protected by other means. All CLUE implementations MUST support DTLS 1.2 with the TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 cipher suite and the P-256 curve, and the SRTP protection profile SRTP_AES128_CM_HMAC_SHA1_80. NULL protection profiles MUST NOT be used for RTP or RTCP, and encrypted header extensions (RFC 6904) MUST be supported.

For privacy, endpoints MUST generate short-term persistent RTCP CNAMEs (RFC 7022) so they cannot be used for long-term tracking of users. The RFC also warns of denial-of-service risks from badly chosen RTCP reporting intervals, and since the CaptureID also appears in CLUE messages, it RECOMMENDS that the SDES item use at least similar protection to the CLUE data channel.
sections.eli5: The video must be sent in a locked box, and the sender must not use a name that follows you from call to call.

fields.name: CaptureID
fields.desc: Variable-length UTF-8 string: a negotiated CaptureID or a single dash.
